title: “THE BIBLE CONTAINS POLYGAMY” IS NOT THE SAME AS “THE BIBLE COMMANDS POLYGAMY”
paragraphs: “THE BIBLE CONTAINS POLYGAMY” IS NOT THE SAME AS “THE BIBLE COMMANDS POLYGAMY”
The Bible Records the Wreckage of Broken People Without Calling the Wreckage Holy—and Jesus Himself Takes Us Back to the Beginning
And with the confidence of someone who thinks they have just discovered Christianity’s fatal contradiction, they say:
Because you have just stepped into one of the most important distinctions you will ever learn when reading Scripture:
The Bible containing something is not the same as the Bible commanding it.
And if you miss that distinction, you can make the Bible endorse almost anything.
It does not therefore command murder.
It does not therefore bless adultery.
The Bible contains incest, drunkenness, betrayal, prostitution, deception, idolatry, violence, cowardice, greed, abuse of power, spiritual compromise, and horrifying human decisions.
Not because God approves of them.
Because God tells the truth about us.
That may be one of the reasons the Bible feels so painfully human.
It does not airbrush its heroes.
It does not Photoshop the patriarchs.
It does not protect kings from embarrassment.
It does not quietly delete the scandals of people God used.
Abraham can believe God and still make disastrous decisions.
Jacob can encounter God and still carry dysfunction into his home.
David can write psalms that have comforted millions and still commit sins that devastate his family.
Solomon can possess extraordinary wisdom and still become a living warning about what happens when wisdom is known but not obeyed.
The Bible does something religious propaganda almost never does:
And that should tell us something.
Scripture is not trying to convince you that biblical characters were flawless.
It is showing you why humanity desperately needs a Savior.
So when someone says, “But Abraham had more than one woman,” or “Jacob had multiple wives,” or “David had several wives,” or “Solomon had hundreds,” the correct response is not to panic.
What does the text actually say about it?
Permission within a fallen social world is not necessarily the Creator’s original design.
And the consequences written into these stories matter.
Before human civilization became tangled in generations of sin.
There, Scripture gives us something remarkably simple.
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
‘Al-ken ya‘azov-ish et-aviv ve’et-immo, vedavaq be’ishto, vehayu levasar echad.
Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother, clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.
And centuries later, when people tried to drag Jesus into a debate about marriage, Jesus did something incredibly important.
He did not begin with Abraham.
He did not say, “Well, Jacob had four women involved in his household, so let us use Jacob as our blueprint.”
He did not point to David's palace.
He certainly did not point to Solomon's enormous household.
Jesus went behind all of them.
The Greek of Matthew 19:5 contains the words:
καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
Kai esontai hoi dyo eis sarka mian.
“And the two shall become one flesh.”
“So they are no longer two, but one flesh.”
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
When human history becomes confusing, He points us toward the Creator's design “from the beginning.”
That is where Christians must begin too.
And suddenly the scandals of the Old Testament start looking very different.
It is sometimes presented casually as evidence that Scripture approves of plural marriage.
Do not merely count the wives.
Children become entangled in their mothers' desperate struggle for affection and status.
A home that should have been a place of covenant peace becomes emotionally fractured.
The Bible does not need a narrator standing over every paragraph shouting, “THIS IS DYSFUNCTIONAL!”
You can hear it in Leah's heartbreak.
You can feel it in Rachel's desperation.
You can watch it spill into the next generation.
That is what careful Bible reading requires.
A man after God's own heart.
The Bible does not hide any of it.
David's greatness does not make every decision David made great.
Being used by God does not mean everything a person does represents the will of God.
That sentence alone could rescue many believers from terrible theology.
God's grace toward a sinner is not God's endorsement of the sinner's every decision.
If biblical polygamy were supposed to be a glorious model, Solomon would be a strange place to make the argument.
He had seven hundred wives of royal status and three hundred concubines.
But Scripture does not finish that sentence with:
“And behold, what a wonderful example of biblical marriage.”
It tells us that his wives turned his heart away.
Long before Solomon's collapse, Deuteronomy 17:17 had already warned Israel's future king not to multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.
The Bible did not command Solomon's excess.
And then recorded what happened when the warning was ignored.
But there is another layer that Christians need to understand.
Some Old Testament laws address situations that already existed in the fallen ancient world.
Regulating a broken situation does not necessarily mean declaring that situation God's ideal.
Sometimes biblical law restrained harm inside circumstances produced by human sin.
Jesus Himself gives us the interpretive principle when discussing divorce.
Moses permitted certain things because of the hardness of human hearts.
But it was not that way from the beginning.
Those words are devastating to shallow arguments built merely on what fallen human beings were permitted or recorded as doing.
That is where Jesus takes us.
Not “What did fallen humanity manage to normalize?”
And this is where this discussion stops being merely about polygamy.
Because you and I do the same thing.
But with our own favorite sins.
We search Scripture for somebody who failed like us and then quietly turn their failure into permission.
And somewhere along the way, grace becomes an excuse for refusing to repent.
Grace does not look at the wreckage and call it beautiful.
Grace walks into the wreckage and begins rebuilding.
Jesus did not come merely to make you comfortable while you remain enslaved to everything destroying you.
And maybe this argument about polygamy exposes something much closer to home.
Because the real question is not simply:
Why are we so eager to use someone else's failure to justify our own?
I have to examine my heart too.
We read about somebody's compromise and think, “See? God still used them.”
But perhaps we have misunderstood the lesson.
“Sin doesn't matter because God uses sinners.”
“Grace is astonishing because God can redeem sinners.”
The Bible's scandals are not embarrassing interruptions in the Gospel story.
They are evidence of why the Gospel is necessary.
Every attempt to manipulate God's promises through human schemes.
They keep whispering the same thing across the centuries:
Abraham could believe and still stumble.
David could conquer armies and still lose battles inside his own desires.
Jesus faced temptation and did not sin.
Solomon possessed wisdom yet allowed his heart to wander.
Jesus is Wisdom incarnate, perfectly faithful to His Father.
The Bible was never ultimately asking you to worship its human heroes.
It was preparing you to recognize the only flawless One when He arrived.
That is why Christianity does not collapse when someone points out the moral failures of biblical characters.
Their failures are part of the case Christianity makes about humanity.
Something has gone terribly wrong inside us.
Even extraordinary wisdom, by itself, cannot cure it.
And that is where the cross enters the story.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die because humanity was basically fine.
He died because sin is deadly.
He opened the way for forgiveness.
The Gospel does not tell scandalous people to pretend they never had a scandal.
It tells them to bring their scandal to Christ.
Then get up and follow Him.
Maybe your story has sexual failure in it.
Maybe choices you would give almost anything to undo.
Maybe you are reading an article about ancient polygamy while carrying a completely different secret.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the door through which you stop running from the One who can heal you.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is restoration for ruined people.
There is a future after failure.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
It means your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final chapter.
That is the heartbeat behind everything we mean when we say:
The Bible is filled with scandals because humanity is filled with sinners.
But the Bible does not end with scandal.
So the next time someone tells you,
you do not have to deny it.
Read Deuteronomy's warning to kings not to multiply wives.
The question is not merely what broken humanity practiced.
The question is what the Creator intended—and where Christ leads redeemed people.
The New Testament continues to point Christian households toward covenant fidelity. Even the qualifications for an overseer use the striking Greek expression:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα — mias gynaikos andra
Literally, a “one-woman man,” commonly rendered “husband of one wife.”
Whatever interpretive discussions surround the precise pastoral application of that phrase, it certainly does not celebrate a man accumulating wives.
The trajectory is not difficult to see.
“The Bible contains polygamy” is not the same statement as “the Bible commands polygamy.”
The Bible is brutally honest enough to record what humans did and holy enough not to confuse everything humans did with what God desires.
And perhaps that is why some passages make us uncomfortable.
The Bible refuses to flatter us.
And then—thank God—it tells the truth about grace.
And if this challenged something in you personally, do not disappear quietly.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read.
Because sooner or later someone will ask this question again.
And when they do, you will want more than a clever comeback.
Not because anyone can buy a blessing.
Give freely, prayerfully, and cheerfully before God.
And there is more waiting for believers who are hungry to grow.
Send it privately to someone wrestling with Scripture.
Comment so others know they are not alone.
Follow so we can keep walking through hard passages together.
Because Christianity was never built on Abraham being perfect.
It stands upon the One who actually is.
The Bible does not hide the scandals of its people.
It reveals the Savior of scandalous people.
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you long after this article disappears from your screen:
God did not preserve their failures so you could imitate their chains; He preserved the truth so you could recognize your need for the One who breaks them.
